prize_parts.citation: for revealing the structure and catalytic mechanism of nitrogenase, the enzyme that reduces atmospheric dinitrogen

statement.case_for: Nitrogenase is a problem of fundamental chemistry that is also a problem of biological energy conversion. A unique iron-molybdenum-sulfur cofactor, with an interstitial carbide, couples ATP hydrolysis, electron transfer and proton delivery to break the N2 triple bond. The MoFe and Fe protein structures, the cofactor composition and the central light atom were established by crystallography and have been confirmed over about three decades. Kinetic and spectroscopic work supplied a physically explicit mechanism. The discovery is clearly attributable, mature and important for chemistry, agriculture and bioenergetics. No earlier prize has covered the enzyme itself, and the committee would be honouring the mechanism behind a process that feeds a large part of humanity. I want the expert reports to confirm that the structure-to-mechanism chain is attributable to three people, and I think it is.
statement.case_against: The catalytic cycle is only partly resolved: the E4 state, the substrate-binding site and the order of proton and electron delivery are still debated, so the committee could be accused of honouring an unfinished mechanism. Credit is also spread across structure (Rees, Einsle), genetics and biosynthesis (Dean, Ribbe) and kinetics (Seefeldt), and the three-person limit forces omissions that will be contested. The candidacy is also much less visible than PROTACs, base editing or lipid nanoparticles, and its practical impact is indirect.

responses.point: Base editing (B019) is chemically explicit, widely used and in the clinic, and a prize would conventionally credit David Liu as the principal investigator, with Komor and Gaudelli as trainees.
responses.response: I ranked B019 fifth, and I agree the deaminase chemistry is explicit and the maturity argument is strong. I disagree that attribution is clean enough for a single name. Kondo and Nishida reported an independent deaminase-based editor, and the committee's own standard is that credit follows the discovery, not the seniority of the laboratory. Whether a Liu-only prize leaves a defensible priority record is something the expert report must settle. I also worry that Chemistry would look like it is recognising the genome-editing field a few years after 2020, when the enzymatic chemistry of nitrogenase has no comparable overlap. I do not rule B019 out and it remains an alternative.

responses.point: Targeted protein degradation (B044) is a new drug modality, built on a clear design principle, and Crews, Deshaies and Handa anchor the PROTAC and molecular-glue strands.
responses.response: This is the strongest-supported candidacy and I take it seriously as the main alternative to mine. My reservations are about attribution and about two strands. The PROTAC concept and the cereblon molecular-glue discovery are different achievements and the credit among Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto, Handa and Ito is crowded. A single three-person citation covering both would be a compromise that neither strand fully earns. A two-part prize would need very careful splitting of three names. The clinical picture is also still incomplete, since I understand no degrader has yet been approved. I would like the expert report to say whether the PROTAC strand and the molecular-glue strand each stand alone.

responses.point: Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (B020) is a clean two-person attribution with four decades of independent use, and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree on attribution: it is the cleanest of the shortlist and the idea is original. I would ask whether it is clearly a chemistry discovery rather than a methods advance whose chemical consequences lie in many different systems, and how far the 2013 multiscale prize already covered the computational territory. The impact argument for B020 rests on a broad body of later work rather than on one chemical finding. This is a fair, serious candidacy, but I do not see a reason for it to outrank a candidate whose mechanism is stated in physical terms. I have not ranked it, so I would like to hear whether you see it as a single achievement or a platform.

responses.point: Biomolecular phase separation (B039) reframes cell organisation as physical chemistry, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the core.
responses.response: I ranked it eighth, though I find the physical-chemistry framing attractive. The question is maturity. You mention yourself that it is disputed which in-cell condensates are truly equilibrium phases, and the quantitative evidence in living cells is thinner than the in-vitro droplet work. I would also want an expert view on whether this is chemistry or physiology. I think the concept is likely to deserve recognition, but I would wait for the interpretation to settle.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports support a three-person nitrogenase configuration of Rees, Einsle and Seefeldt, or favour a different allocation among structure, genetics and mechanism.
Whether the incomplete N2-reduction mechanism is judged mature enough for recognition now.
Whether B044 should be split into PROTAC and molecular-glue parts, and if so how three names are divided.
Whether B019 priority (Liu versus Kondo and Nishida) can be settled from the record.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows a scientific proximity to B032 as a biochemist working on biological energy conversion and proton transfer in respiratory enzymes, which is a field interest rather than a personal or institutional tie to any credited person. I am also a Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou, who has no credited candidate in my configuration. No specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile.
